title: Sharding
summary: Split data across independent stores only when one database cannot keep up.
keyPoints: Sharding splits one logical data set across independent stores.
The shard key decides which queries are single-shard and which fan out.
Hash, range, and directory routing trade balance, range efficiency, and control.
Hot keys overload one shard even when the key distribution is even.
Cross-shard queries and transactions add latency, partial failures, and coordination.
Exhaust indexes, caching, replicas, and vertical scale before sharding.

complexity.note: Requires the shard key in the query.
Results need merging and partial-failure handling.
Good for ordered scans, risky for monotonic writes.
Throttle the copy and keep a rollback path.

commonMistakes: Sharding before trying query tuning, caching, or read replicas.
Choosing a low-cardinality shard key that creates a few huge shards.
Using a time-based key for a write-heavy table and sending every new row to one shard.
Assuming a cross-shard join or transaction will behave like a single-database one.
interviewNotes: State the shard key and the main query it makes cheap.
Name the queries that must fan out and how you merge or avoid them.
Say how unique ids are generated across shards.
Explain how you would reshard without downtime.

checkYourself.question: What makes a good shard key?
checkYourself.answer: High cardinality, even storage and access, stability, and alignment with the most common query so requests touch one shard.

checkYourself.question: Why does adding read replicas not fix a write bottleneck?
checkYourself.answer: Replicas copy writes from the primary. Every write still passes through the primary, so replicas add read capacity, not write capacity.

checkYourself.question: What is a hotspot and one way to reduce it?
checkYourself.answer: A key or shard that receives far more traffic than the others. Cache the hot value, split the key into sub-keys, or give the hot object dedicated capacity.
